PART V - PARLIAMENT [Article 79-122]

Parliamentary system borrowed from UK (Westminster Model).

Article 79 - Constitution of Parliament

  • There shall be a Parliament of India that consists of:
  • The President and;
  • Two Houses:
  • Council of States (Rajya Sabha) - Upper House
  • House of the People (Lok Sabha) - Lower House

Lok Sabha (LS):

  • First sitting: 13 May 1952
  • Constituted on: 17 April, 1952
  • is also known as the 'House of the People' (Hindi name adopted in 1954)
  • Members elected directly by the people.

Rajya Sabha (RS):

  • First sitting: 13 May 1952
  • Constituted on: 3 April, 1952
  • is also known as the 'Council of States' / 'Permanent House' (Hindi name adopted in 1954)
  • Represents States.
  • Also known as the 'House of Elders'
Themes of New Parliament buildings:
Lok Sabha: Peacock
Rajya Sabha: Lotus

President is an integral part of Parliament. No Bill becomes law without his assent.

Article 80 - Composition of Council of States (Rajya Sabha)

  • Total Members (Maximum 250):
  • 238 elected members
  • 12 nominated by the President: From the fields of - Literature, Science, Arts, Social Service (LISAS)
  • Present strength of RS: 245 (233 elected, 12 nominated)
  • 5 seats are vacant for PoK, Aksai Chin, etc.

Representation in RS:

  • Members are indirectly elected by means of Proportional Representation and Single Transferable Vote (STV)
  • Note: Unequal representation in RS (based on population) (e.g., UP - 31 seats, small States like Sikkim/Goa etc. - 1 seat each).
  • Election of RS members is borrowed from South Africa.
  • Nomination of RS members is taken from Ireland.

Article 81 - Composition of House of the People (Lok Sabha)

  • Total Members (Maximum 550):
  • 530 from States
  • 20 from Union Territories
  • Present strength: 543 elected members
2 Anglo Indians were nominated by President, this provision was removed later through 104 CA, 2019.

Representation in LS:

  • Direct election by citizens.
  • Parity maintained among Inter and Intra States.
Q. Do you know why Lok Sabha has green carpet and Rajya Sabha has red Carpet?
Ans: Green colour represents that India is an agricultural land and people here elected from grassroots level.
Red colour represents royalty and symbolises the sacrifices done by the freedom fighters and the blood they shed to gain independence for India.

Article 82 - Readjustment after Each Census

Delimitation Commission established after every Census (10 years) to:

  • Divide constituencies based on population.

Important Delimitation Acts: 1st in 1952, then 1962, 1972, 2002.

Key Amendments:

  • 42th CA (1976): Seats were fixed based on 1971 Census until 2000.
  • 84th CA (2001): Freeze on Delimitation Commission extended till 2026.
  • 87th CA (2003): Minor adjustments, Delimitation according to 2001 Census.
"Delimitation" means the act or process of fixing limits or boundaries of territorial constituencies.

Article 83 - Duration of Houses

Rajya Sabha:

  • Permanent body; not subject to dissolution
  • 1/3rd members retire every 2 years;
  • Term of members of RS is 6 years.

Lok Sabha:

  • Tenure: 5 years.
  • Can be extended during national emergency (one year at a time).
  • Elections must be held within 6 months after the end of emergency.
Requirement for a candidate contesting election to RS from a particular state should be an elector in that particular state was dispensed with in 2003.

Article 84 - Qualifications for Membership of Parliament

  • Must be a citizen of India.
  • Minimum required age: 30 years (Rajya Sabha), 25 years (Lok Sabha)
  • Other qualifications as prescribed by Parliament.

Article 85 - Sessions of Parliament, Prorogation, and Dissolution on the advice of Council of Ministers.

Parliamentary Sessions: (summoned by the President)

  • Budget Session: February to April
  • Monsoon Session: July - August
  • Winter Session: December
Note: Maximum gap between sessions cannot exceed 6 months.

(Continuation of Article 85)

  • Prorogation: Ends a session (by President).
  • Dissolution: Formal termination of the current Lok Sabha session (by President).
  • Adjournment: Temporary break within a session where a sitting is terminated (by Presiding Officer).
  • Adjournment Sine die: by Presiding Officer
  • Ends the session meeting without fixing a date for next session, happens just before prorogation.
  • The adjournment motion is introduced in the Parliament to draw the attention of the house to a definite matter of urgent public importance and needs the support of 50 members to be admitted.

Some other Parliamentary motion/Procedures:

  • Closure Motion: A motion moved by a member to cut short the debate on a matter before the house.
  • Call Attention Motion: It is introduced in Parliament by a member to call the attention of a minister on a matter of public importance.
  • Point of Order: It is raised when the proceedings of the house do not follow the normal rules of procedure. No debate is allowed on Point of Order.

#### Censure Motion vs No-Confidence Motion

Censure MotionNo-Confidence Motion
Reason must be statedNo reason required
Can be moved against an individual, group, or entire councilCan be moved against entire council only.
To target for some specific policies/actionsTo test majority support (confidence) of LS in CoM.
If passed - no resignation requiredIf passed - resignation is mandatory

Types of Questions:

  • Starred: Oral question-answers, can have supplementary questions.
  • Unstarred: Required written answers, no Supplementary questions could follow.
  • Short Notice: 10 days prior notice should be given.
  • Question could also be asked to private members.
  • (A private member is the one who is not a minister.)
Routine of a session:
11 AM: Start
11 AM - 12 PM: Question Hour
12 - 1 PM: Zero Hour (Agenda of the day is decided)

Article 86 - Right of President to Address and Send Messages

  • President can address either House or both Houses jointly.
  • President can send messages regarding pending Bills or other matters.

Article 87 - Special Address by the President

  • President addresses both Houses: At the first session after each general elections and the first session of each fiscal year.
  • Motion of Thanks follows the address.

Article 88 - Rights of Ministers and Attorney General

  • Right to speak in either House but can vote only in that house of which they are a member.
  • Attorney General is not a member of either house but has the right to speak in LS/RS, without having Right to Vote.

Officers of Parliament:

Article 89 - Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha

  • Chairman: Vice President of India (Ex-officio). He is not a member of RS.
  • Deputy Chairman: Elected by Rajya Sabha.
  • Fulfills duties as the Acting Chairman in absence of the Chairman. He is a member of RS.
  • While the Chairman is presiding the house, he is like any other member of the house.

Article 90 - Vacation, Resignation, Removal of Deputy Chairman

  • Resignation: by writing to the Chairman.
  • Removal by Effective majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha. (Effective Majority = Majority of the total membership of house - Vacancies)

Article 91 - Power/Duty of Deputy Chairman

  • Presides in absence of Chairman.
  • When Seats of C and Dep. C are vacant: then President can choose any member from the house to discharge duties of RS.
  • If the Chairman and DC, both are absent, then: one member of the Panel of Vice-Chairpersons, appointed by the Chairman, presides. (This is not explicitly mentioned in Constitution).

Article 92 - Chairman and Deputy Chairman Not to Preside During their removal

  • They can participate in proceedings but cannot preside during their own removal resolution.
  • Can vote in first instance but not in the case of tie (casting vote exercised by Presiding Officer).
  • Chairman does not have the casting vote rights in this case, as he is not a member of RS.
P.T. Usha: first woman to be appointed in the RS panel of Vice-Chairpersons.

Article 93 - Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha

  • Elected by Lok Sabha members by Simple Majority
  • First Speaker: Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar.
  • First Deputy Speaker: M. A. Ayyangar.
  • Note: No Deputy Speaker appointed since 2019.

Article 94 - Vacation, Resignation, Removal of Speaker and Deputy Speaker

  • Resignation: Speaker resigns to Deputy Speaker and vice-versa.
  • Removal: by Effective majority.
  • Speaker continues till a new Speaker is elected.
  • He does not immediately resign after the dissolution of LS and continue till the newly elected LS meets.
Date of election of Speaker is fixed by the President, and that of deputy speaker is fixed by speaker.

Article 95 - Powers to Perform Duties

  • Deputy Speaker presides when Speaker is absent.
  • If the Seat is vacant: then President can choose any member to discharge the duties.
  • If the speaker and Deputy speaker, both are absent, then: one member of the Panel of Chairpersons, appointed by the Speaker presides.

Article 96 - Speaker and Deputy Speaker Not to Preside During Their Removal.

  • They can participate but cannot preside while a motion for their removal is under discussion. (The Speaker's right to vote in the first instance is retained, but has no right to casting their vote in the case of tie.)
  • Note: Deputy speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker.

Article 97 - Salaries and Allowances

  • Salaries of Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha - are decided by Parliament.

Article 98 - Secretariat of Parliament

  • Each House has its separate secretarial staff.
  • Secretariat appointed by President on advice of the Speaker of the LS and Chairman of RS.

Article 99 - Oath or Affirmations by Members

  • Every member of either House must take oath before taking his seat as administered by the President or a person appointed by him.
  • Protem Speaker: Senior-most member appointed temporarily by President to administer oath to members.

Article 100 - Voting in Houses and Quorum

  • 100(1) The Chairman or Speaker shall not vote in the 1st instance but shall exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
  • 100(3) Quorum: Minimum 1/10th of total strength of House is required to carry on the proceedings.
  • 100(4) If quorum is not met, house is adjourned by the presiding officer.

Article 101 - Vacation of Seats

  • 101(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament.
  • 101(2) No person can be a member of State Legislature and a member of Parliament.
  • 101(3) Members can be disqualified as mentioned in Article 102
  • (3A) A member can resign his seat to the Chairman or Speaker.
  • 101(4) If a member of either of the Houses of Parliament is absent without permission for a period of 60 days, the house may declare the seat vacant.
RPA: Representation of People Act, 1951
Jail for more than two years lead to disqualification.

Article 102 - Disqualifications for Membership

102(1): A person shall be disqualified for membership if:

  • (a) He holds any office of profit under the Union or State Government.
  • (b) He is of unsound mind, as declared by a competent court.
  • (c) He is an undischarged insolvent.
  • (d) He is not a citizen of India.
  • (e) He voluntarily acquired citizenship of another country or allegiance to a foreign State.
  • (f) He is so disqualified under the 10th Schedule.

102(2): Disqualification under 10th Schedule - Defection

On the grounds of:

  • Independent members join any political party.
  • Nominated members join the political party after 6 months from the date of his nomination.
  • If he votes contrary to the direction of his party.
  • If the member voluntarily gives up the membership of the party on whose ticket he has been elected.
  • Exception: Merger when 2/3rd members leave and join other political party (91st CA, 2003)
Decision of the Speaker is final with regard to disqualification under defection.
Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu Case: Judiciary can review the final decision of the Speaker in case of disqualification under Defection.

Article 103 - Decision on Questions of Disqualification

  • 103(1) Decision of the President shall be deemed final if question arises over disqualification of any member of the either house.
  • 103(2) President must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission before giving his final decision.

Article 104 - Penalty for Sitting and Voting When Disqualified or before making an oath or affirmation under Article 99

  • If any person sits or votes knowing they are disqualified, a penalty of Rs. 500 per day is charged for the period he/she sat or voted.

Article 105 - Powers, Privileges, and Immunities of Parliament Members

  • 105(1) Freedom of speech in Parliament.
  • 105(2) No proceedings in Parliament can be questioned in any court of law. No MP liable for anything said or any vote given in Parliament.
  • 105(3) MPs enjoy protection from civil arrest during a session and 40 days before and after the session (by parliamentary convention).
  • This protection does not apply to criminal arrest or preventive detention.
  • (Note: Protection of the President from criminal proceedings is under Article 361, not Article 105)

Article 106 - Salaries and Allowances of Members

  • Parliament may by law fix salaries and allowances of members of both the Houses.

LEGISLATIVE PROCEDURES

Article 107 - Introduction and Passing of Bills

  • 107(1) A Bill can originate in either House (LS or RS) except the Money bill.
  • 107(2) A Bill passes if both Houses agree, with or without amendments.
  • 107(3) Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse due to adjournment or prorogation of the session.
  • 107(4) Bills lapsing after dissolution:
  • A Bill pending in Lok Sabha and not passed at the time of its dissolution lapses.
  • A Bill pending in the RS, which has not been passed by the LS shall not lapse on the dissolution of the LS.

Types of Bills (Diagram)

  • Citizenship Amendment Bill
  • Constitutional Amendment Bill
  • Ordinary Bill
  • Public Member Bill (1 week prior notice should be given)
  • Private Bill (brought by a MP who is not a minister) (1 month prior notice should be given)
  • Financial Bill
  • Money Bill

Passage of Ordinary Bill:

  • can originate in either house.
  • If both the houses pass the bill, it goes to President for his Assent.
  • When Deadlock created → President calls Joint Sitting → Bill passed by Simple Majority.
Deadlock is created in 3 cases.
  • (a) the bill is rejected by the other house; or
  • (b) the houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the bill; or
  • (c) more than six months, elapse from the date of the reception of the bill by the other house without the bill being passed by it.
  • To resolve the deadlock, the President may summon a joint sitting.

Article 108 - Joint Sitting of Both Houses

  • 108(1) In case of a deadlock (disagreement between both Houses), the President may summon a Joint Sitting.
  • 108(2) Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over the Joint Sitting.
  • In his absence Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides.
  • In absence of both → Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha. (Chairman cannot preside the Joint sitting as he is not the member of either house.)

Exceptions: Money Bill and Constitutional Amendment Bill - No Joint Sitting allowed.

  • Simple majority is needed to pass the Bill (majority of members present and voting).
  • Joint Sitting follows the Rules of Lok Sabha.
Provision of Joint sitting is taken from Australia.

Joints Sittings has happened 3 times till now:

  • Dowry Prohibition Bill, 1960
  • Banking Services Commission Bill, 1977
  • Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 2002

Article 109 - Special Procedure for Money Bills

  • 109(1) A Money Bill can only be introduced in Lok Sabha, on the recommendation of the President.
  • 109(2) After a bill is passed to RS, it can: approve, suggest amendments or take no action on the bill but it must give its response within 14 days.
  • 109(3) Lok Sabha may accept or reject Rajya Sabha's suggestions.
  • If RS does not pass the bill within 14 days → It shall be deemed passed by both Houses.

Article 110 - Definition of Money Bill

A Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only provisions related to:

  • (a) Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, regulation of any tax.
  • (b) Regulation of borrowings.
  • (c) Custody and audit of Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund.
  • (d) Appropriation of money out of Consolidated Fund.
  • (e) Declaring any expenditure as charged on Consolidated Fund.
  • (f) The receipt of money into the Consolidated Fund of India or the Public Account of India, or the custody or issue of such money.
  • (g) Any matter incidental to any of the above matters.
The Speaker of Lok Sabha certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
  • The Speaker's decision is final, and normally cannot be challenged in any court. However, Judicial review is allowed.
A Bill is not considered as a money bill if it provides:
For the imposition of fine/imposition or abolition of any tax by local Authority.

Article 111 - Assent to Bills

  • After a bill is passed by both the Houses the bill is then presented to the President.
  • President may:
  • (a) Give assent - Bill becomes a law.
  • (b) Use its Veto power.

Veto powers of the President (Negative Powers)

  • Absolute Veto: President rejects the Bill completely.
  • Suspensive Veto: President returns the Bill for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, assent is mandatory.
  • Not available in case of Money bill because it is already brought into the Parliament after the prior recommendation of the President.
  • Pocket Veto: No action taken by President. (No time limit to act.)
  • This veto was first used by Giani Zail Singh for Indian Post Office (amendment) bill 1986.
No Veto can be used in case of a Constitutional Bill: 24th CA (Article 368)
Pocket of Indian President is deeper than the USA's president because no time limit is mentioned in constitution for Indian president to act on the bill.

Article 112 - Annual Financial Statement (Budget)

  • President shall cause to be laid before both the Houses, a statement of estimated receipts and expenditures.
The term 'Budget' is not mentioned in the Constitution.

Article 113 - Procedure in Parliament with Respect to Estimates

  • No expenditure from Consolidated Fund of India be done except with the authorization by Parliament.
  • Estimates of Expenditure are divided into two parts:
  • Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (not votable due to salaries of President, SC judges, etc.)

(Continuation of Article 113)

  • Made from the Consolidated Fund of India (subject to vote in Lok Sabha through Demands for Grants).
  • Only Lok Sabha has the right to vote on Demands for Grants. RS can only discuss it.
  • Demands for Grants are presented on behalf of the President.

Article 114 - Appropriation Bills

  • The Appropriation Bill is introduced to authorize the withdrawl of money from the Consolidated Fund of India.
  • No amendments or voting on the Appropriation Bill amounts - it is passed as a formality after Demands for Grants are voted.
  • Cut motions are moved during the voting on Demands for Grants:
  1. 1. Policy Cut: Reduce the amount to Rs. 1 to criticize government policy.
  2. 2. Economy Cut: Reduce by a specified amount to suggest savings.
  3. 3. Token Cut: Reduce by Rs. 100 to raise a specific grievance.

Article 115 - Supplementary, Additional, Excess grants

  • Supplementary grant: granted when the amount authorised by Parliament is found insufficient.
  • Additional grant: granted for additional expenditure upon some new service.
  • Excess grant: It is granted when money has been spent on any service in excess of the amount granted to that service in the budget.

Article 116: Vote on Account, Votes of Credit, and Exceptional Grants

Vote on Credit:

  • Financial grant given to the Executive from India's resources to meet urgent financial needs.
  • Details cannot be shared ordinarily in a budget.
  • It acts like a blank cheque given to the Executive by the Lok Sabha (LS).

Exceptional Grants:

  • Special provisions made by Parliament.
  • Used to meet specific expenses not covered under the regular budgetary allocation.

Stages in enactment of budget

  1. 1. Presentation
  2. 2. Discussion
  3. 3. Scrutiny by departmental committees
  4. 4. Voting on demands for grants
  5. 5. Passing of Appropriation bill
  6. 6. Passing of Finance bill

Different Types of Funds

  1. 1. Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266)
  • Consists of: Tax & Revenue
  1. 2. Public Account of India (Article 266)
  • Consists of: Remittance (public fund deposits) and Judicial deposits
  • Managed by: Executive (not under Parliament's direct control)
  1. 3. Contingency Fund of India (Article 267)
  • In hands of President but run by President and Finance Secretary.

Article 117: Special Provisions for Financial Bills

  • All Money Bills are Financial Bills, but vice versa is not true.
  • Procedure of financial bill is same as ordinary bill, except that financial bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha and with prior recommendation of President.

Article 118: Rules of Procedure

  • Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business.

Article 119: Regulation of Procedure for Financial Business

  • Parliament can regulate laws related to financial procedures.

Article 120: Language to be Used in Parliament

  • Business of Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or in English.
  • Unless Parliament by law provides, Use of 'English' to be removed after 15 years.
  • Presiding officer may allow any member to express themselves in their mother tongue.

Article 121: Restriction on Discussion in Parliament

  • No discussions shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court.

Article 122: Court not to Inquire into Proceedings of Parliament

  • No court shall inquire into Parliament proceedings.
  • Conduct of MPs or officers not subject to court jurisdiction.

Article 123: Power of President to Promulgate Ordinances during Recess

  • President can issue ordinances when both Houses are or even one House is not in session.
  • Ordinance has same force as an Act of Parliament.
  • (a) Must be laid before both Houses shall cease to operate after 6 weeks from reassembly unless approved.
  • (b) Can be withdrawn anytime by the President.
  • Ordinance should not contain provisions beyond Parliament's legislative competence (i.e. on the subjects of union list.)
  • Legislative power of President (Centre) under Article 123;
  • Legislative power of Governor (State) under Article 213.

Max Life of an Ordinance:

  • Approved → Continues as law.
  • Disapproved → Ordinance lapses.
  • In case, Parliament takes no action: max life - 6 months and 6 weeks, How?
  • Max gap between sessions: 6 months,
  • When no action is taken: 6 weeks post reassembly.
DC Wadhwa Case vs State of Bihar, 1986: Relates to misuse and repeated re-promulgation of ordinances.

Special Powers of Rajya Sabha

  1. 1. Can authorise Parliament to create a new All India Service (Article 312)
  2. 2. Can authorise the Parliament to make a law on a Subject of State List. (Article 249)

PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES

  • Constitution mentions these committees at different places but without any specific provision regarding their tenure, functions, etc.
  • All these matters are dealt by rules of two houses.
  • A Parliamentary committee is appointed by Speaker / Chairman and works on his directions.

Classification of Parliamentary Committees

  • Permanent Committee
  • Standing Committee
  • Temporary Committee
  • Ad Hoc Committee

#### Financial Committees

  • Public Accounts Committee
  • Estimates Committee
  • Committee on Public Undertakings

Public Accounts Committee:

  • Established in 1921 through GOI Act 1919.
  • Total members: 22 members (15 from LS + 7 from RS).
  • Guide and Philosopher: CAG (submits reports which are analysed by PAC).
  • Function: To examine the audit reports of CAG.

Estimates Committee:

  • Established in 1921.
  • Re-established post Independence: 1950 on recommendation of John Mathai Committee.
  • Total members: 30 (all from LS), (increased from 25 to 30 in 1956).
  • Function: To examine estimates included in budget.

Committee on Public Undertakings:

  • Established in: 1964 on recommendation of Krishna Menon Committee.
  • Total members: 22 Members (15 from LS + 7 from RS) (Increased from 15 to 22 in 1974)
  • Chairman is from Lok Sabha.
  • Function: To examine reports and accounts of Public Undertakings.

Similar features of all the Financial Committees:

  • Election: Proportional representation - STV (Single transferable vote)
  • Appointed/elected by the House or nominated by Speaker/Chairman.
  • Term of members: 1 year
  • No Minister can be a member. (Only private member)

Departmental Standing Committees

  • Total: 24 (16 from LS + 8 from RS)
  • Strength: 31 members (21 from LS + 10 from RS)

Speaker of Lok Sabha is the Chairman of:

  • Business Advisory Committee
  • Rules Committee
  • General Purpose Committee
Deputy Speaker is a member of Committee on Private Members Bill (He automatically becomes the Chairman of any Committee he/she is appointed as a member of).
